document.title: S/P Ambassador Haass' Call on [Excised] (Islamabad 09489)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), "No-Go" Tribal Areas Became Basis for Afghan Insurgency Documents Show
document.note: [Secret] Richard Haass meets an unnamed Pakistani military official on October 31, 2002. The official claims there are no al-Qaeda safe havens in Pakistan and that al-Qaeda's tribal-area presence is limited to transit. Haass says al-Qaeda's core is in Pakistan and the threat is as large as on September 10. The official describes FATA's maliks-versus-mullahs conflict and the former "no-go areas" opened briefly after Tora Bora when tribes were overawed by U.S. firepower; "that window [is] closed."

events.description: Haass met a senior Pakistani (name excised) who assured him of the Army's commitment to counterterrorism and disputed al-Qa'ida presence in Pakistan.
Embassy Islamabad sent the cable reporting the Haass call to Washington.
Tora Bora operation; Pakistan Army deployed along border opposite with local leaders' cooperation.
S/P Director Richard Haass called on a Pakistani official (excised) in Islamabad and was assured of the Army's commitment to counterterrorism.
Embassy Islamabad sent cable 09489 reporting the Haass call to Washington.
During the Tora Bora operation the Pakistan Army deployed along the border opposite Tora Bora with local leaders' cooperation.
Ramzi bin al-Shibh was captured in Pakistan.
Abu Zubaida was captured in Pakistan.
Announcement of India-Pakistan troop pullbacks from the border, welcomed by Haass.
Haass met a Pakistani interlocutor (excised) and discussed al-Qa'ida's presence in Pakistan, India-Pakistan de-escalation, and Kashmir.
Haass said he was pleased by the announced troop pullbacks from the India-Pakistan border, which would free resources for sealing the Afghan border and counter-terrorism.
Pakistan's interlocutor asked the US to provide an aerial surveillance capability and proposed giving the same to India as a confidence-building measure.
Embassy Islamabad transmitted cable 09489, reporting Haass's call, to Washington.

relationships.detail: The Army official said the Army had no sympathy for al Qaeda and supported the US-led war on terrorism.
relationships.quote: THE ARMY HAD NO SYMPATHY FOR AL QAEDA

relationships.quote: THE ARMY HAD PROACTIVELY BEGUN TO OPERATE IN THE FATA, USING DEVELOPMENT PROJECTS AND ROAD BUILDING

relationships.quote: DURING THE TORA BORA OPERATION, THE ARMY HAD DEPLOYED ALONG THE BORDER OPPOSITE TORA BORA

relationships.detail: The Army claimed it was in total agreement with the US on ends in the war on terrorism, though it differed on methods.
relationships.quote: PAKISTAN,S MILITARY WAS IN TOTAL AGREEMENT WITH THE US ON "ENDS,"

key_claims: Pakistan's Army claimed full agreement with the US on ends but differed on means, preferring long-term ties with tribes.
A Pakistani interlocutor asserted there were no al-Qa'ida safe havens in Pakistan and that al-Qa'ida controlled no part of FATA, only transiting.
US operations in Afghanistan briefly opened a window for the Pakistan Army to enter FATA 'no-go areas', which had since closed.
The US view was that al-Qa'ida's core was in Pakistan, had reconstituted and posed a threat as large as on 9/10.
Pakistani side said mullahs in NWFP/FATA were al-Qa'ida sympathizers but could not shelter them for more than a day or two.
Pakistan said operations based on bad US intelligence alienated NWFP Pashtuns and asked for specific actionable information.
Pakistan requested US aerial surveillance capability and suggested sharing it with India as a confidence-building measure.
